details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

MarsWalk is an offline planner for a two-person walk on Mars ("Marswalk") at the boxwork ridges of Mount Sharp, Gale Crater, where Curiosity drove in 2025. It answers four questions a crew must settle before and during an EVA: which science stops are worth the energy, which route a suited human can walk, when they must turn back, and what to do if one astronaut is injured or a solar storm starts.

A Python pipeline clips real NASA data to a 3 km x 3 km site and builds a 3 m walking grid: slope, roughness, boulder shadows, terrain sky cover, a science score from CRISM sulfate and ridges, and a DEM quality flag. On this site 24.4% of the ground is steeper than 20 degrees and cannot be walked.

An engine in a Web Worker does all the calculations:

- Route: A* search where each step costs metabolic energy (Santee et al. 2001 load-carriage model at Mars gravity). Uphill costs more than downhill, so the way out and the way back differ. Slopes of 15-20 degrees cost extra; over 20 degrees is a wall.

- Walk-back area: a Dijkstra search from the habitat over reversed edges gives the energy and time to get home from every cell. It shrinks as the EVA clock runs.

- Science planner: adds the stop with the most science value per extra joule while the plan keeps the energy reserve, EVA time and walk radius. On the real site: 6 Curiosity stops and 2 science-value peaks, 4.86 km, 3 h 54 min, 6.00 MJ of a 7.60 MJ budget.

- Contingencies: if B is injured at EVA time 1:30, A carries B to the habitat (1.47 km, 39 min, 1.85 MJ), with B's mass as load in the same model; if the habitat is out of reach, A goes to the nearest rover pickup zone. In a solar particle alert, the crew goes to the nearest full shelter (habitat or rover).

- Buddy tracking: a warning when the two astronauts are more than 100 m apart.

The app shows the HiRISE orthophoto with every data layer, the route, an elevation and energy profile, an EVA timeline, both crew positions, and a high-contrast helmet mode with large buttons, spoken answers and optional voice commands.

BENEFITS

- One map at the scale a person walks, instead of regional maps.

- Data from several NASA missions on one grid, in one view.

- Plans around human limits: slope, body energy, time, the walk back and the buddy rule.

- Answers in seconds without Earth: radio signals take 3 to 22 minutes each way, and the app runs fully offline after the first load.

INTENDED IMPACT

Mission planners and future crews could use it to check an EVA plan before leaving the habitat, and to re-plan on the spot when something goes wrong. The same pipeline works for any site that has a HiRISE elevation model, so it could support landing-site and EVA studies for human missions.

TOOLS

Python 3.11 (rasterio, numpy, scipy, pytest) for the data pipeline; TypeScript in a Web Worker for the engine; Vite, Leaflet and vite-plugin-pwa for the app; Vitest for tests; GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for deployment. No server, no backend, no paid APIs. It runs in any modern browser on a laptop or tablet. Code, tests and docs were written with Claude Code (Anthropic) under the team's direction.

CREATIVITY

- Direction matters: costs are directional, so the walk-back area is computed over reversed edges.

- Rescue without invented factors: the injured astronaut's mass is carried as load in the same model.

- Real Curiosity stops become the science stops, each shown with the Navcam photo taken there.

- Helmet mode turns the plan into a glance-and-go display for gloved hands.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Trust: every number on screen comes from a calculation or a constant with a source. Constants that are our own choice are labelled "assumption" next to every value that uses them, and users can change the adjustable ones and see everything recalculate.

- Real data only: no synthetic terrain. A strip of the DEM with seam artefacts is flagged as low confidence by a measured test.

- Safety limits: terrain gives only partial radiation shielding, so only the habitat and rover count as full shelters.

- Honest limits: crew positions and the solar storm are simulated (the storm quotes the measured May 2024 RAD value), and the energy model comes from tests on Earth, scaled to Mars gravity.

- Quality: 145 automated tests check the physics rules (uphill costs more than flat ground and flat more than a moderate downhill, no route crosses a slope over 20 degrees, the safe area shrinks over time, a rescue costs at least as much as walking, results are repeatable).
